prompt: The operations team (4 people) of an online payment processing company collects application logs from its payment API servers in a single Amazon CloudWatch Logs log group, and three weeks of logs have accumulated so far. After an incident yesterday in which errors spiked, management asked for the number of ERROR entries over the past 7 days right now, and going forward the team must be notified through an existing Amazon SNS topic when there are more than 20 ERROR entries within 5 minutes. The historical count is a one-time request, and the company does not want to build a separate pipeline to move the logs to another system. The operations team has no dedicated developers. The log group's retention period is already 30 days, so all three weeks of logs are still available, and the report to management is needed this afternoon. Which combination of steps meets both requirements with the LEAST development effort? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increase the log group's retention period so that a metric filter re-evaluates the historical logs, and generate the metric for the past 7 days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because a metric filter is applied retroactively to existing logs, query the same filter metric to check the number of ERROR entries over the past 7 days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a new metric filter for the ERROR pattern, and create an alarm that goes to the ALARM state when the 5-minute sum of that metric exceeds 20, with an SNS notification attached.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a CloudWatch Logs Insights query to filter the ERROR events from the past 7 days and count them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Create a subscription filter to resend the existing logs to Amazon Data Firehose, and count the entries from the past 7 days by using Amazon S3 and Amazon Athena.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination that handles the historical count with a Logs Insights query and handles future notifications with a metric filter and an alarm. Logs Insights queries logs that are already stored on demand, so it fits the past-7-days count. According to the documentation, a metric filter publishes metrics only for events that occur after the filter is created, so it takes care of the forward-looking threshold alarm. The claim that a filter is applied retroactively to existing logs is not true. Increasing the retention period does not cause a filter to re-evaluate past logs. A subscription filter delivers log events in real time as they are ingested, so it is not a means of retroactively sending logs that have already accumulated, and setting up Athena as well increases the development effort.

prompt: An internal order-processing web server (one EC2 instance with the SSM Agent and the CloudWatch agent installed) at a logistics company went down twice in the early morning last month because temporary files piled up and filled the disk. The company now wants an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to run without human intervention to clean up old temporary files when the disk usage alarm goes to the ALARM state. The alarm has already been created from CloudWatch agent metrics, and a standard runbook that runs without a reboot is ready for the cleanup. No one is on call overnight, and the burden of writing new code must be kept to a minimum. The cleanup path is already set as a runbook parameter, and this server's IAM instance profile has Systems Manager permissions attached. Which configuration is MOST suitable?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Specify running the SSM Automation runbook directly as an EC2 action in the existing alarm's alarm actions, connecting it in one step without a separate rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Wrap the alarm in a composite alarm, and specify running the cleanup runbook as the composite alarm's Systems Manager action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receive the alarm notification by SNS email, have an engineer review it and run the SSM Automation runbook manually from the console, and record the execution result in a ticket. Document the details in a wiki for post-incident review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receive the alarm state change event with an Amazon EventBridge rule that matches when the state is ALARM, and specify the SSM Automation runbook as the target.

explanation: The correct answer is the configuration that receives the alarm state change event with an EventBridge rule and specifies SSM Automation as the target. CloudWatch sends an event to EventBridge every time an alarm changes state, and a rule that matches only the ALARM state can run the runbook without any code. The direct actions of a standard metric alarm are SNS notifications, EC2 actions, and Auto Scaling actions, and none of them lets you specify running a runbook directly. The Systems Manager action of a composite alarm is for creating OpsItems or incidents and does not run runbooks. Receiving an email and then running the runbook manually violates the requirement for no human intervention.

prompt: The security team at a fintech startup was cited in an external audit last quarter for leaving one Amazon S3 bucket accidentally open to public read access for three weeks. The team now wants any bucket policy change that would allow public read access to be blocked automatically, without human intervention. The scope is several hundred buckets in a single account, and auditors must be able to query the configuration change history and compliance status later. Checks and remediation must run continuously, including outside business hours, and the security team does not have enough staff to maintain code themselves. No bucket needs an exception to be public, and the on-duty security engineer works under the condition of not being called at night. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Receive AWS CloudTrail events with Amazon EventBridge, and implement a custom-written AWS Lambda function that parses the bucket policy, determines whether it is public, and blocks it. Record the compliance history in a separate Amazon DynamoDB table that you build yourself for querying.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable the AWS Config managed rule (s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited) and attach automatic remediation that uses an SSM Automation document.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty to send an alert email when a public bucket is found, and have an engineer block public access on that bucket from the console.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Check the AWS Trusted Advisor results every day, and have an engineer manually find the buckets flagged as public and block public access.

explanation: AWS Config evaluates bucket configurations with a managed rule and retains the compliance status and change history, and attaching an SSM Automation document as a remediation action lets it fix noncompliant resources automatically. A custom Lambda function requires you to implement and maintain the policy-parsing logic and exception handling, and you would also have to build the compliance history yourself. Having an engineer block the bucket after a GuardDuty alert, and checking Trusted Advisor every day, both require human intervention, so they fail the requirement to block automatically and the requirement to query compliance history.

prompt: At 10:12 AM, a developer accidentally dropped the orders table in a production Amazon RDS for MySQL database (Multi-AZ deployment) at an online shopping company. Automated backups are turned on with a 7-day retention period, and the data as of 10:10 AM, just before the deletion, must be recovered. The shopping site is otherwise operating normally, and new data keeps accumulating in the payments and inventory tables even after the deletion, so that data must not be lost. The recovery must be performed with minimal service interruption. Only one table needs to be recovered, its size is a few GB, and the developer reported the deletion immediately. What is the MOST appropriate recovery method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run a point-in-time restore on the production instance to roll the same instance back in place to its 10:10 AM state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a point-in-time restore to 10:10 AM to create a new DB instance, export the orders table from the restored copy, and load it back into the production database.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run a failover to the Multi-AZ standby and promote the standby, which still holds the data from before the deletion, to be the new primary instance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Restore the latest daily snapshot to create a new instance, switch the service to that instance's endpoint, and then change all application connection strings. Have an engineer review the changes before the switchover.

explanation: The correct answer is to create a new instance with a point-in-time restore and reload only the needed table. According to the documentation, a point-in-time restore does not modify the source and always creates a new DB instance, and because transaction logs are uploaded every 5 minutes, you can restore to a point in time such as 10:10 AM. Rolling the same instance back in place is not offered and would also lose the latest data in the other tables. The standby is replicated synchronously, so the drop command has already been applied to it. A daily snapshot would lose all table changes made after the snapshot, which violates the requirements.

prompt: A logistics software company wants to enable communication among 12 VPCs used by different accounts and teams in the same Region, and 2 to 3 VPCs will be added each quarter. The CIDR blocks of all the VPCs do not overlap. There are only two network administrators, so the company wants to reduce the number of connections and the routing configuration to manage, and the effort required to attach a new VPC must also be small. Most inter-VPC communication consists of small API calls, and there is no requirement for internet-bound traffic or on-premises connectivity. Each VPC is owned by a different team, so every routing change request requires an approval process, and the total traffic volume is modest at a few hundred GB per month. Which configuration has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a VPC peering connection for every pair of VPCs to configure 66 peering connections, and add a route to the peer CIDR in each VPC's route table.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peer one hub VPC with each of the other VPCs, and configure an EC2 proxy in the hub to forward traffic, working around the transitive routing limitation of peering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a transit gateway and attach each VPC to it, and centrally manage the routes between VPCs by using the transit gateway route table.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Attach a virtual private gateway to each VPC and connect the VPCs to one another with site-to-site VPN tunnels to create encrypted paths between VPCs, managing BGP routing for each tunnel yourself.

explanation: The correct answer is a transit gateway hub configuration. A transit gateway is a hub that connects VPCs and on-premises networks, each VPC needs to create only one attachment, and routes are managed centrally in the route tables, so the workload grows only linearly as VPCs are added. Peering all 12 VPCs would require 12×11÷2 = 66 connections plus route table changes on both sides, and this would grow sharply as VPCs are added. VPC peering does not support transitive routing, so a configuration that goes through a hub VPC requires you to operate EC2 proxies yourself, which become a bottleneck and a point of failure. VPN between VPCs is the most complex because you must manage both the tunnels and the devices.

prompt: The platform team at a SaaS company deploys the network layer by using a nested stack template that is shared by multiple product teams. During a routine check, the team ran drift detection on the parent stack and the result was IN_SYNC. However, it was later discovered that someone had directly changed the inbound rules of a security group created by a child stack from the console. There are too many stacks for people to inspect the console one by one, and the team must find such changes without exception going forward. The security group change in question has already occurred once, and the audit team has requested a per-stack report if the same type of change occurs in the future. What is the MOST appropriate method for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because drift detection on the parent stack does not cover the nested stacks, run drift detection directly on each nested stack as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If you run drift detection on the parent stack repeatedly, the results of the child stacks are merged into the parent result over time, so run detection frequently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because drift detection supports only EC2 instance resources, security group changes can be monitored only with AWS Config rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If you use a stack policy to deny updates to security group resources, console changes are also blocked, so drift cannot occur.

explanation: When you detect drift on a parent stack, CloudFormation does not detect drift on the nested stacks that belong to it, and you must initiate the detection operation directly on each nested stack. Therefore, running detection on each child stack is the correct answer. Running it repeatedly does not merge the child results into the parent result. Drift detection works across supported resource types, including security groups, not just EC2, so the claim that the support is limited to EC2 is not true. A stack policy controls only stack update operations and cannot prevent directly changing resources through the console or the API.

prompt: The site of an e-commerce company has a core revenue path that runs from logging in to adding an item to the cart. Last month, because of a misconfiguration on the login server, users could not add items to their carts for 3 hours in the early morning, but the health checks on the target servers were all normal, so no one noticed. The company must verify every minute, even in the early morning when there is almost no traffic, that this flow works from a real user's perspective, and an alarm must fire if it fails. The check results must be kept as CloudWatch metrics, and the company must not operate servers for the checks itself. It would be good for the canary results to leave evidence such as screenshots, but this is not required, and the incident response owner receives notifications by SNS email, not SMS. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use an Amazon Route 53 health check to check the HTTP response code of the login page URL, and send an alarm when the health check fails.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create an alarm on the HealthyHostCount metric of the ALB target group, and treat a decrease in the number of healthy targets as an outage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary as a multistep script with a 1-minute schedule, and set an alarm on the canary's success rate metric.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Place a cron-based curl script on a separate EC2 instance, upload the results as a CloudWatch custom metric, and set an alarm on it.

explanation: The correct answer is a CloudWatch Synthetics canary. A canary is a script that runs on a schedule and follows the same paths and actions as a customer, it can run as often as every minute, it works even when there is no traffic, and you can set an alarm on its success rate metric. A Route 53 health check looks at the result of a single URL request, so it cannot verify a multistep flow from login to the cart. The number of healthy targets on an ALB only shows whether servers respond and does not tell you whether the user flow succeeds. The EC2 with cron approach violates the requirement because you would have to operate a server for the checks yourself.

prompt: A media company processes image conversion jobs that accumulate in an Amazon SQS queue by using 40 worker instances in an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. The jobs are idempotent, a job that is interrupted during processing is processed again from the queue, and it is acceptable for results to be several hours late. The workers do not store state locally, and the units of work are split into short pieces. Compute costs exceeded the budget last quarter and the finance team demanded savings, and the team wants to solve this with purchasing options and configuration alone, without changing the workload code. A single job finishes in 2 minutes on average, and the workers currently all use one single instance type and run On-Demand. Which method reduces cost the MOST while securing capacity reliably?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Purchase 3-year All Upfront Standard Reserved Instances for 40 instances' worth of capacity and run all workers as Reserved Instances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lease a Dedicated Host, consolidate the 40 workers onto it, and reduce instance costs with host-level pricing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Consolidate the workers into 10 larger On-Demand instances to reduce the number of instances and the number of servers to manage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a Spot Instance configuration with multiple instance types and Availability Zones specified in the Auto Scaling group, and let interrupted jobs be processed again after the SQS visibility timeout.

explanation: Spot Instances let you use spare EC2 capacity at a large discount, but the capacity can be reclaimed when it is needed again. This workload is idempotent, stateless, and delay-tolerant, and it is reprocessed through SQS, so it can tolerate interruptions. Mixing multiple instance types and Availability Zones makes the workload less sensitive to a capacity shortage in any single pool, which makes it easier to secure capacity. A 3-year All Upfront Reserved Instance commits to a long term for a batch workload that varies greatly and tolerates delay, and its discount is smaller than Spot. Dedicated Hosts are used when licensing or regulatory requirements demand them and are not a way to reduce cost. Consolidating into larger On-Demand instances gives no unit-price discount, so the cost savings are limited.

prompt: The on-call team at an online gaming company wants to receive an SNS paging notification only when the web server CPU utilization alarm and the ALB 5xx error count alarm are both in the ALARM state at the same time. Both alarms have already been created, but a page goes out when only one of them fires, and over the past month there have been more than 20 unnecessary early-morning pages, which has greatly increased team fatigue. Pages for cases where only one alarm fires must be reduced. The team must not write new code or operate separate servers, and it must keep using the existing SNS topic for notifications. The evaluation periods of the two alarms are the same at 5 minutes each, and the PagerDuty integration for paging is already subscribed to the SNS topic. What is the MOST appropriate method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a composite alarm that references the two alarms, set the rule expression to an AND of the ALARM conditions of the two alarms, and attach the SNS action only to the composite alarm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach the same SNS topic to each of the two alarms, and have the engineer who receives the notification check whether the other alarm has also fired and then manually page the on-call engineer only when necessary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an EventBridge rule for each of the two alarms that matches events whose state is ALARM among the alarm state change events, and specify the same SNS topic as the target.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower the threshold of the CPU alarm and lengthen the evaluation period of the 5xx alarm so that the times at which the two alarms change state overlap and the SNS notifications go out together.

explanation: The correct answer is a composite alarm. A composite alarm does not evaluate metrics directly but evaluates a rule expression that references the states of other alarms, and the expression can use the AND, OR, and NOT operators and state functions such as ALARM, so the composite alarm goes to ALARM only when both alarms are in ALARM, and the SNS action can run at that time. Attaching SNS to each alarm sends a notification even when only one fires and leaves a manual checking step for a person. An EventBridge rule matches one event at a time, so the target runs as soon as either alarm goes to ALARM, and the rule cannot express a simultaneous condition. Adjusting thresholds and evaluation periods only changes alarm sensitivity and does not logically combine the notification conditions.

prompt: An Amazon S3 bucket at a healthcare data company contains about 40 million objects that were stored without encryption. A new regulation requires that all objects be encrypted with SSE-KMS and that key usage be auditable through AWS CloudTrail, and the audit is next month. New objects continue to be uploaded to this bucket, and the upload application is difficult to modify. Because of the large number of objects, processing them manually one by one is not realistic, and the operations team has 3 people. Versioning is turned off on the bucket, and the external partners who upload do not include an encryption option in the request headers. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set the bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS, since existing objects are automatically re-encrypted, and wait without any additional work after changing the setting. Periodically check that newly uploaded objects are handled the same way.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Set the bucket default encryption to SSE-KMS to handle new objects, and use an S3 Batch Operations copy job to create encrypted copies of the existing objects.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use a lifecycle rule to transition the existing objects to the S3 Standard-IA storage class, because they are encrypted with KMS during the transition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a bucket policy that denies unencrypted upload requests, so that existing objects are automatically encrypted the next time they are accessed.

explanation: The default encryption setting applies only to new objects uploaded afterward, and objects that are already stored are not encrypted, so existing objects must be processed by creating encrypted copies with S3 Batch Operations. Simply changing the default encryption to SSE-KMS does not re-encrypt the 40 million existing objects. A storage class transition does not change an object's encryption method. A bucket policy only inspects upload requests and does not apply encryption when stored objects are read. When you create copies with a batch job, they are encrypted with the key that you specify.

prompt: The infrastructure team at a company received a report that connections on port 443 to an EC2 web server in a newly created subnet are failing. This subnet has a custom network ACL applied to meet security requirements. The security group allows inbound 443 and allows all outbound traffic. The network ACL has only an inbound allow rule for 443 and an outbound allow rule for 443. The VPC flow logs record the 443 traffic from the client to the server as ACCEPT and the response from the server to the client's ephemeral port as REJECT. The team has checked the server's OS firewall and the application settings and found no problems, and other servers in the same subnet show the same symptom. What is the MOST appropriate action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add a rule to the security group outbound rules that explicitly allows TCP traffic to the ephemeral port range.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add a rule to the network ACL outbound rules that allows TCP traffic to the ephemeral port range (1024-65535).

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the number of the network ACL inbound 443 rule to a lower number to raise its rule evaluation priority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add an explicit route for the client CIDR range to the subnet route table so that the response traffic can return.

explanation: The correct answer is to allow the ephemeral port range in the network ACL outbound rules. Network ACLs are stateless, so the response to an allowed inbound request must be allowed separately by an outbound rule, and the combination of request ACCEPT and response REJECT in the flow logs points to exactly this situation. Security groups are stateful, so responses are allowed automatically, and because all outbound traffic is already open, adding a rule would have no effect. The request is already ACCEPT, so the inbound rule number is not the problem. For responses within the same VPC the local route already exists, so adding a route is not the solution.

prompt: A manufacturing company wants to automatically install security patches every Sunday on EC2 instances spread across 25 accounts and 4 Regions in AWS Organizations, and on several hundred on-premises servers registered through Systems Manager hybrid activation, and to view compliance status in one place. The company wants to avoid repeating the same configuration in every account and Region. The patch schedule is managed by the central security team, not by the owners of each account, and it would be good if the same policy applied when a new account is added to the organization. Patching starts at 2:00 AM on Sunday and requires one reboot per server, and the on-premises servers are already registered as Systems Manager managed nodes. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Systems Manager Quick Setup, configure a patch policy targeting the organization, and specify the installation schedule and the patch baseline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create maintenance windows in each account and Region, and run the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document as a Run Command task on the schedule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Configure the Quick Setup Host Management option for the entire organization, and set the weekly patch installation schedule with this configuration.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have the owner of each account and Region manually run a Patch now operation with Scan and install every Sunday.

explanation: A Quick Setup patch policy integrates with Organizations, so a single policy can define the schedule and patch baseline and target multiple accounts and Regions across the organization, or even only some OUs, and it can run scanning and installation on different schedules. A task in Maintenance Windows targets only a single account and Region combination, so the configuration has to be repeated for each account and Region. The Host Management option is limited to scanning for missing patches and creating reports and cannot install patches. Patch now also targets only one account and Region at a time and is run manually without a schedule, so it does not meet the requirements.

prompt: A company runs its web service in the Seoul Region with an Application Load Balancer and an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group. Currently the subnets are in only one Availability Zone, so during a recent AZ failure the service was down for about 2 hours. Going forward, the service must stay available even if one AZ fails completely, and the capacity of the failed AZ must be restored automatically in the remaining AZs. The company wants to solve this mainly by changing settings of the existing configuration without redesigning the architecture, and no one is on call overnight. The service does not store state on local disks, sessions are stored in Amazon ElastiCache, and the database is already configured as Multi-AZ. Which TWO actions meet these requirements with the LEAST change? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Upgrade the instance type to one twice as large as the current type and place more instances within a single AZ to reduce the chance of a single-instance failure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Configure the ALB across subnets in the same three AZs and associate the Auto Scaling group with the target group so that requests go to targets in the healthy AZs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the minimum capacity of the Auto Scaling group to 0, and when an AZ failure is detected, have an operator add a subnet in a new AZ from the console to restore capacity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Associate an Elastic IP address with the EC2 instances, and prepare a procedure and checklist in which an engineer manually moves the address to a standby instance in another AZ during a failure. Also run switchover drills regularly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Specify subnets in three different AZs for the Auto Scaling group to distribute instances across the AZs, so that capacity is replenished in the remaining AZs when an AZ fails.

explanation: The correct answer is the combination that configures both the Auto Scaling group and the ALB across multiple AZs. When the group uses subnets in multiple AZs, it launches new instances in the unaffected AZs when an AZ becomes unhealthy and rebalances evenly after recovery, and the load balancer must also enable the same AZs so that traffic goes to targets in the healthy AZs. According to the documentation, an ALB must enable at least two AZs. Scaling up or adding instances within the same AZ does not protect against an AZ failure. A minimum capacity of 0 with manually adding subnets, and manually moving an Elastic IP address, depend on human response rather than automatic recovery.

prompt: The platform team at a SaaS company is looking for a way to prevent a recurrence after an incident in which a production CloudFormation stack was accidentally deleted. The stack contains about 40 resources, including an Amazon RDS database, an ALB, and an Auto Scaling group, and a CI/CD pipeline updates the stack several times a day. Going forward, attempts to delete the stack must fail, but stack updates resulting from template changes must remain allowed through the pipeline without being blocked, as they are now. The template is shared across several parts of the team, so the team wants to avoid any method that significantly changes the template structure. The stack deletions were mostly caused by developers clicking by mistake in the console, and the pipeline uses its IAM permissions only for stack updates. What is the MOST appropriate method that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Set DeletionPolicy: Retain on all resources in the stack so that the resources remain even if the stack is deleted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use a stack policy to deny Update actions on all resources.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enable termination protection on the stack.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on the disable rollback option when creating the stack so that the stack cannot be deleted.

explanation: When termination protection is enabled, deletion attempts fail and the stack and its state are kept as they are, and it does not affect updates, so it meets both requirements together. DeletionPolicy: Retain only leaves the resources behind when the stack is deleted and does not prevent deletion of the stack itself. Denying all updates with a stack policy would block the CI/CD updates that happen several times a day, which violates the requirement. Disable rollback is an option about automatic rollback when creation fails, which is a different feature from termination protection, and it does not prevent deletion.

prompt: A total of 200 EC2 instances in private subnets at a video analytics company download about 5 TB per day from an Amazon S3 bucket in the same Region. They currently connect through a NAT gateway, so data processing charges account for a large share of the monthly cost, and the finance team asked to reduce this item. All the clients are inside the VPC, and access from on premises is not needed. S3 access permissions are already granted through IAM roles, and all the objects are in a bucket in the same Region. The application code must not be changed. All S3 access is based on IAM roles, and the bucket policy does not yet have a condition that allows only a specific VPC. Which method is the MOST cost-effective and the simplest to configure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an S3 interface endpoint in each subnet and turn on private DNS so that S3 requests go to the endpoint ENIs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add one NAT gateway per AZ to distribute data processing throughput and reduce inter-AZ data transfer charges.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the application settings to use the S3 Transfer Acceleration endpoint to optimize the transfer path.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create an S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the route tables used by the private subnets.

explanation: The correct answer is to associate an S3 gateway endpoint with the route tables. According to the documentation, a gateway endpoint lets you reach S3 without an internet gateway or NAT device and has no additional charge, so it eliminates the NAT data processing charges while satisfying the requirement that access come from within the VPC. An interface endpoint carries hourly charges and data processing charges, which is an unnecessary cost in this situation. Adding NAT gateways increases hourly charges and leaves the data processing charges unchanged. Transfer Acceleration is for improving upload speed over long distances and does not reduce NAT costs.

prompt: The operations team at a financial services company wants to keep the CloudWatch agent installed and running on EC2 instances tagged Env=prod (about 150 instances that grow and shrink frequently with Auto Scaling). Even if someone stops the agent or a new instance with the same tag is added, the instances must return to the desired state within a set interval, and compliance must also be verifiable. The agent configuration uses a standard document defined by the security team, and all instances are managed by Systems Manager. The installation document is already registered as a Systems Manager document, and the agent configuration is set up to read values from Parameter Store. Which method has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run the install command once with Run Command, and then have an engineer periodically check for later changes and rerun it if needed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a State Manager association on a set schedule that runs the agent installation and configuration documents against the target tag.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Register a task that runs once a month in a maintenance window so that the agent is reinstalled on a set day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Put a script that checks the agent status via cron on each instance, collect the results directly through Lambda, and build a report.

explanation: A State Manager association keeps applying a document to target nodes on a set schedule to maintain the desired state, and when you target by tag, instances added later are included as well and compliance status is reported. State Manager is the right tool for automating system compliance, and Maintenance Windows is the right tool for time-sensitive tasks in a set time window. Running Run Command once does not restore later changes or cover new instances, and it requires people to check. A once-a-month task could leave a stopped agent unattended for up to a month, which does not meet the requirement to recover within a set interval. Self-built cron and Lambda increase the operational burden even though a managed feature exists.

prompt: The web service of an online education company runs on multiple instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. Last night the web process died on one instance and it returned only HTTP 503. The EC2 status checks all passed, so the group marked the instance as healthy, and the ALB reported the target as unhealthy, but the group did not replace the instance. The company does not want to repeat this situation, in which the on-call engineer had to terminate the instance manually in the early morning. The target group health check is already configured to expect a 200 response on the /health path, and the instance warmup time after launch is appropriately set to 300 seconds. What is the MOST appropriate action to have failed instances replaced automatically without changing application code?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduce the health check interval of the ALB target group to 5 seconds and lower the unhealthy threshold count so that an instance is judged unhealthy more quickly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase the health check grace period so that the group waits longer after an instance launches before it starts health checks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run a Lambda function on an EventBridge schedule that analyzes the ALB access logs and terminates the instance when 5xx errors increase, and let the group refill the terminated instance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Additionally turn on the Elastic Load Balancing health check type for the Auto Scaling group so that instances the ALB considers unhealthy are replaced.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on the Elastic Load Balancing health check type for the group. By default, Auto Scaling uses only EC2 status checks and ignores the load balancer health check results, so if the EC2 checks pass it does not replace an instance even when the process has died. When the ELB checks are turned on, an instance that the load balancer reports as unhealthy is marked unhealthy at the next check and replaced. Shortening the target group health check interval is useless if the group does not use that result. The grace period only delays when checks begin right after launch and has no effect on a failed instance that is already running. The access log and Lambda approach must be built and operated yourself.

prompt: The operations team at a retail company applies patches to 12 EC2 web servers behind an ALB only between 02:00 and 04:00 every Saturday. Before patching, each instance must be deregistered from the load balancer, and the order of re-registering it after patching must be guaranteed, and no work may start outside that time window. This is a time-sensitive task that runs in a set time window, and the team does not want to build an orchestration server that it operates itself. All the instances are managed by Systems Manager, and the team has 3 members. The load balancer deregistration step proceeds in batches of 3 instances at a time, and even if a patch fails, the remaining batches must continue. What is the MOST appropriate method that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create a maintenance window with a Saturday 02:00 schedule and a 2-hour duration, and register as a task an AWS Step Functions Standard state machine that defines the order of deregistration, patching, and re-registration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document periodically with a State Manager association to patch all 12 instances at the same time all at once. Check the execution results per instance in the State Manager compliance report.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Use Patch now to run Scan and install on all 12 instances at once, and after it completes, have a person check the load balancer registration status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Configure the patch installation schedule for the entire organization with the Quick Setup Host Management option, and have the installation run on early Saturday morning.

explanation: Maintenance Windows is a tool that runs potentially risky tasks at set times by specifying a schedule and a maximum duration, and a Step Functions task can orchestrate the sequence of removing a node from the load balancer, patching it, and adding it back (only Standard state machines are supported). A State Manager association is intended for maintaining state and compliance, so it does not fit this task that requires control of the time window and ordering, and patching the instances at the same time could interrupt the service. Patch now is a manual immediate run that ignores schedules and does not guarantee the deregistration and re-registration order. The Host Management option is limited to scanning for and reporting missing patches and cannot install patches.

prompt: Forty CloudWatch Logs log groups used by multiple Lambda functions and Amazon ECS services at a media streaming company have never had their settings changed since creation, and they are driving up monthly costs. Under the audit policy, logs only need to be retained for 90 days and can be deleted after that. All the log group names start with /app/, and it would be good if the same policy also applied to log groups created with this prefix in the future. The operations team has no capacity to write code. Some of the log group names keep increasing as new services are added, and the company has confirmed that deleting logs older than 90 days causes no regulatory problem. What is the MOST efficient way to reduce cost without writing code?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Configure an EventBridge scheduled rule and a Lambda function to delete the 40 log groups every month and recreate them with the same names.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run an export task to Amazon S3 every day for each log group, and leave the logs on the CloudWatch Logs side as they are with no further action after exporting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create an account-level retention policy that specifies a 90-day retention period for the /app/ prefix, and set it to a mode that also applies retroactively to existing log groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the default retention period of log groups is already 90 days, leave the log group settings as they are and add only an S3 lifecycle rule.

explanation: The correct answer is to create an account-level retention policy for the /app/ prefix with 90-day retention in retroactive mode. CloudWatch Logs stores logs indefinitely by default, so you must specify a retention period to reduce costs, and a prefix-based account-level policy applies to all 40 groups at once without code, and retroactive mode (RETROACTIVE) also applies to existing groups (the policy takes effect about 24 hours after it is created, and expired events are not deleted immediately but can take up to about 72 hours). Deleting and recreating log groups every month would also erase logs within the 90 days needed for the audit. An S3 export only copies the logs and does not reduce the cost of retaining the originals. The premise that the default retention period is 90 days is wrong, because the default is never expire, so an S3 lifecycle rule has nothing to do with CloudWatch Logs costs.

prompt: A global retail company has 70 accounts in AWS Organizations, and the audit team wants to collect management events from all enabled Regions in all accounts into a single Amazon S3 bucket. Newly created accounts must be included automatically, and administrators of member accounts must not be able to turn off or change the trail. Under company policy, logs are kept centrally in only one place, and the audit team has no staff to check the settings in each account. The organization's management account is operated separately by the security team, and CloudTrail trusted access is already enabled. Which method meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deploy a trail with the same settings to each account by using StackSets, and have all the trails deliver logs to the central S3 bucket.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Have the audit team export each account's CloudTrail Event history by hand every 90 days and collect it in the central bucket.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a single-Region trail in the management account, and bring in and retain events from other Regions by using S3 Cross-Region Replication.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a multi-Region organization trail in the management account or a delegated administrator account, and deliver the logs to the central S3 bucket.

explanation: An organization trail is created in the management account or a delegated administrator account and logs events from all member accounts of the organization to a single bucket, and it is applied automatically when a new account is added to the organization. Users in member accounts can only view the organization trail and cannot delete it, turn off logging, or change it. An organization trail created in the console is a multi-Region trail that covers all enabled Regions. Trails deployed to each account with StackSets can be modified or turned off by member account administrators. Exporting Event history is manual and limited to a 90-day range. A single-Region trail does not record activity in other Regions, so it cannot be supplemented with replication.

prompt: A mobile gaming company runs 60 Linux EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group. The operations team must be notified when memory utilization exceeds 85%, but it cannot find a memory item in the default EC2 metrics in the console. Instances are replaced frequently as traffic changes, so configuring each instance by hand must be avoided, and security policy does not allow SSH access to the instances to be left open. An SNS topic for notifications already exists. All the instances run Amazon Linux, and the instance profile already has CloudWatch agent permissions attached. Which configuration has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on EC2 detailed monitoring so that the 1-minute default metrics include memory utilization, and set an alarm on that metric to notify through SNS.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a metric filter on the application log group to calculate system memory utilization, and set an alarm on the metric that the filter creates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include the installation and configuration of the CloudWatch agent in the launch template so that it publishes a memory utilization metric, and set an alarm on that metric to notify through SNS.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run a Lambda function every 5 minutes that connects to each instance over SSH, reads the output of the free command, and sends an SNS notification when the threshold is exceeded.

explanation: The correct answer is the configuration that deploys the CloudWatch agent through the launch template to publish a memory metric and sets an alarm on that metric. The default AWS/EC2 metrics include CPU, network, and disk throughput, but not memory utilization inside the guest OS, so an agent is required, and putting it in the launch template applies it automatically to replacement instances with no manual work. Detailed monitoring only shortens the collection interval from 5 minutes to 1 minute and does not add a memory metric. A metric filter extracts values from log strings and does not calculate OS memory utilization. The Lambda and SSH approach has the largest burden because you must also operate key management and handling of connection failures yourself.

prompt: A company that operates an internal HR system wants to use an internal Application Load Balancer in the Seoul Region as the primary endpoint and an internal Application Load Balancer in the Tokyo Region as the secondary, and to switch the access of corporate VPN users with failover routing in an Amazon Route 53 private hosted zone. The ALBs have no public IP addresses and the security groups allow only the VPC-internal CIDR range, and the security team does not allow exposing the ALBs to the internet for health checks. Switchover during a failure must happen automatically without human intervention. The ALBs in both Regions serve an application with the same configuration, and user traffic must normally go only to Seoul. What is the MOST appropriate way to have Route 53 determine the state of the primary endpoint?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an endpoint health check that targets the private IP address of the primary ALB and associate it with the failover record.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a CloudWatch alarm on a metric such as the ALB's HealthyHostCount, and associate a Route 53 health check that monitors that alarm with the failover record.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Specify the ALB DNS name as the target of an endpoint health check, shorten the check interval to a fast 10 seconds, lower the failure threshold count, and associate it with the record. Also publish the check results to a separate dashboard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to weighted routing instead of failover, and prepare a runbook for manually changing the weight of the primary record to 0.

explanation: The correct answer is to create a Route 53 health check that monitors a CloudWatch alarm. According to the documentation, endpoint health checks send requests from Route 53 over the internet, so they cannot reach an internal ALB that has no public IP address, and such private resources are evaluated with a health check based on a CloudWatch alarm. An endpoint check that targets a private IP address or the ALB DNS name will always fail for the same reason, even if you shorten the check interval. Weighted routing and a manual runbook are not automatic failover, so the switchover is tied to the speed of human response.

prompt: A healthcare information company must encrypt all of its EBS volumes to meet a compliance requirement. The Seoul Region currently has 20 production instances with unencrypted volumes attached, and volumes that team members create in the future must be created encrypted without mistakes. Developers create new volumes themselves with the console and the CLI. Existing volumes can be replaced during a monthly maintenance window, but service interruption at any other time is not allowed. For the AWS CloudTrail audit evidence to pass, the Encrypted attribute of every EBS volume must be true, and using AWS managed keys is allowed. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the KMS key attached to the existing volumes to a customer managed key so that the unencrypted volumes become encrypted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable EBS encryption by default in the Seoul Region.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because enabling encryption by default automatically encrypts existing volumes that are already attached, wait without any additional work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create a snapshot of each existing volume, create a new encrypted volume from that snapshot, and replace the existing volume with it during the maintenance window.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turn on the encryption attribute for the existing volumes with ModifyVolume to encrypt the volumes in place without stopping the instances.

explanation: The correct answers are turning on encryption by default and creating new encrypted volumes from snapshots and swapping them in. Encryption by default makes newly created volumes, and volumes created from unencrypted snapshots, encrypted, but it does not change volumes that already exist. An existing unencrypted volume cannot be encrypted directly, and you must create a snapshot and create a new encrypted volume from it. ModifyVolume changes the type, size, and performance, so it cannot turn on the encryption attribute. An unencrypted volume has no KMS key to change, and the key of an existing volume cannot be changed. The claim that encryption by default applies retroactively to existing volumes is not true.

prompt: An accounting software company has a group of EC2 instances whose CPU utilization is high only in the last week of each month because of quarter-end close processing. When the company turned on AWS Compute Optimizer in the middle of this month, it produced an over-provisioned finding and a recommendation for an instance type one size smaller, but the team is concerned that the month-end load may not have been reflected. If month-end processing slows down, it directly affects customers' closing schedules, so performance risk must be reduced, and simply keeping the instances large is not consistent with the cost goal. All of these instances are of recent-generation types, memory metrics are not yet being collected, and changes can be made only after month-end processing. What is the MOST appropriate action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Opt out of Compute Optimizer and opt in again at month-end so that it newly collects only the metrics from the month-end load period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If you add memory metrics with the CloudWatch agent, the analysis period of Compute Optimizer is automatically extended to more than one month.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activate enhanced infrastructure metrics so that it looks at 93 days, which is longer than the default recommendation analysis period of 14 days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ignore the recommendation and move all instances up to a type one size larger to match the month-end load, preventing performance problems.

explanation: After you opt in, Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics over a default period of 14 days, and turning on enhanced infrastructure metrics (a paid feature) extends the analysis period for the selected resources to 93 days so that it can reflect the monthly cycle. Opting out and opting in again does not make use of analysis history and would actually hinder the accumulation of metrics. Memory metrics can improve the accuracy of recommendations but do not change the analysis period. Ignoring the recommendation and running larger instances goes in the opposite direction of the goal of reducing costs.

prompt: Account A at an insurance company has an Amazon EBS snapshot encrypted with a customer managed AWS KMS key, and for a disaster recovery drill the snapshot must be restored to a volume in account B. The snapshot has already been shared with account B, but when an administrator in account B tried to restore it, a KMS permissions error occurred. The security team does not allow making the snapshot public or removing its encryption, and both accounts belong to the same AWS Organizations organization. The restore is performed by a specific IAM role in account B. The snapshot in account A is already shared with account B, and the account B role already has the EC2 and EBS related permissions. Which TWO actions are required to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reapply the snapshot sharing setting, because granting the snapshot sharing permission again also delegates access to the KMS key.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attach an IAM policy that delegates kms permissions on the account A key ARN to the IAM role in account B that performs the restore.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Change the snapshot sharing setting to public, because it can then be restored from any account, and do not deal with KMS permissions separately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add a statement to the key policy of the account A KMS key that allows account B (or a specific role in account B) to use the key.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Change the KMS key associated with the snapshot in place to a key owned by account B to remove the dependency on the existing key.

explanation: The correct answers are allowing account B in the key policy and delegating that permission with an IAM policy in account B. Cross-account KMS use requires both the key policy in the account that owns the key and an IAM policy in the external account, and one of the two alone is not enough. An encrypted snapshot cannot be made public and can be shared only with specific accounts, and the security team also prohibits making it public. The KMS key of an existing snapshot or volume cannot be changed, and it can be switched to a different key only during a copy. Sharing a snapshot is only a permission on the snapshot and does not automatically grant KMS key permissions.

prompt: The security team at an e-commerce company newly enabled AWS Security Hub CSPM and turned on the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard. The findings from Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Inspector appeared immediately, but even after several days almost no security control check results have been generated for Amazon S3 and IAM. The account uses only a single Region, Seoul, and the team uses only AWS services without any separate third-party security tools. The status of the account's AWS Config recorder has not been checked yet, and there is talk that the company ran without turning on AWS Config because of cost. What is the MOST likely cause of this problem and its solution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CloudTrail data events are turned off, so enable S3 data event logging and connect the logs to Security Hub CSPM.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The 30-day free trial of Security Hub CSPM must end before control checks begin, so wait for the trial period to pass.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cross-Region aggregation is turned off, so specify an aggregation Region and configure it to receive control results from all Regions in one place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: AWS Config is not turned on or is not recording resources, so enable Config recording in that account and Region.

explanation: For most controls, Security Hub CSPM runs its checks by using AWS Config service-linked rules, so control results are generated only when Config is turned on and recording resources. The findings from GuardDuty and Inspector are sent by other services, so they appear regardless of Config. CloudTrail data events are not a prerequisite for control checks. The free trial period concerns billing, and checks run even during the trial. Cross-Region aggregation is a feature that shows results from multiple Regions in one place and does not itself produce control checks.

prompt: During a disaster recovery drill at a financial company, a database was brought up on a gp3 volume created from a 4 TB encrypted EBS snapshot, and during the first few days the latency was high each time a block was read for the first time, so the recovery time objective (RTO) was not met. A single snapshot is used for recovery, and recovery is set to be performed in only one AZ in the Seoul Region. A new snapshot is created once a day, and the database instance type cannot be changed. The snapshot lifecycle is managed with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM), and the recovery drill runs once per quarter. Which method provides full volume performance right after restore while minimizing additional cost?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restore with the volume type changed to io2 and specify the maximum provisioned IOPS so that the latency of first-time block reads disappears.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enable fast snapshot restore in all AZs in the Seoul Region and apply the same setting to all the snapshots you hold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Move up to an instance type with greater EBS-optimized bandwidth so that the first-read speed of the restored volume increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable fast snapshot restore for that snapshot only in the one AZ where recovery will be performed.

explanation: The correct answer is to turn on fast snapshot restore only for the needed snapshot and a single AZ. This feature fully initializes volumes created from the snapshot at creation time, which eliminates the latency on first reads of blocks and matches the symptom exactly, and because an hourly charge applies for each snapshot and AZ combination, limiting it to the one snapshot and one AZ used for recovery gives the lowest cost. The volume type and provisioned IOPS are performance factors separate from the latency of fetching snapshot blocks for the first time. Enabling it for all AZs and all snapshots only adds cost and goes beyond the requirement. Increasing instance bandwidth still leaves the first-access latency.

prompt: The operations team at a SaaS company wants to know in advance about hardware retirement and maintenance events that AWS has scheduled for the EC2 instances in its account, and wants to send automatic notifications to an Amazon SNS topic connected to the company's internal messenger. Last quarter instances restarted without warning and customer inquiries increased. The company must avoid installing an agent on every instance for the notifications, and the scope is a single account. The notification channel is already consolidated into an SNS topic, and the target instances include standalone instances outside Auto Scaling groups. Retirement notices usually arrive several weeks in advance, and when the team receives one, it responds by stopping and starting the instance itself during a maintenance window. Which configuration has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Create an alarm on each instance's StatusCheckFailed metric to notify the SNS topic when a status check fails.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Use an EventBridge rule to match AWS Health scheduled change events for EC2, and specify the SNS topic as the target.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Query the CloudTrail event history every day to see whether there were retirement-related API calls, and have an engineer share them manually in the messenger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Check the Trusted Advisor results screen once a week, download the list of instances scheduled for retirement, and forward it to the messenger by hand.

explanation: The correct answer is the configuration that receives AWS Health events with an EventBridge rule and delivers them to SNS. Health emits scheduled changes to account resources as events, and the documentation also describes using SNS and other targets from an EventBridge rule, so this gives advance notification without an agent. A status check failure alarm fires after a problem has already occurred, so it cannot give advance notice of the schedule. CloudTrail is a record of API calls by users and services, not a maintenance notice that AWS has scheduled. Periodically checking the Trusted Advisor screen requires continuing manual work.

prompt: A log analysis pipeline at a telecommunications company performs large sequential reads from a dedicated data volume (12 TiB) on EC2 and must continuously sustain a throughput of about 400 MiB/s. There is almost no random I/O, and this volume is not a boot volume. Most read operations happen in large blocks of 1 MiB or more. The company currently uses an SSD volume, so storage cost has become a burden, and latency is not important. The volume is attached to only a single instance, the instance type is a large type with sufficient EBS throughput, and the read block size is consistently 1 MiB or more. Which EBS volume type meets the required throughput at the LOWEST cost?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An st1 Throughput Optimized HDD volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: An sc1 Cold HDD volume, to get the lowest cost per GiB

choices.label: C
choices.text: A gp3 volume with throughput provisioned at 400 MiB/s or higher

choices.label: D
choices.text: An io2 Block Express volume with IOPS provisioned to match the required throughput

explanation: st1 is an HDD designed for large sequential workloads such as big data and log processing. Its baseline throughput is 40 MiB/s per TiB, so a 12 TiB volume sustains 480 MiB/s even without burst credits, and the per-volume maximum is 500 MiB/s, so it meets the requirement to sustain 400 MiB/s while costing less than SSD. The condition that it is not a boot volume allows HDD to be used. sc1 has a baseline throughput of 12 MiB/s per TiB and a maximum of 250 MiB/s per volume even with burst, so even at 12 TiB it reaches only 144 MiB/s and falls short. gp3 can reach up to 2,000 MiB/s, but as an SSD its unit price is higher, so it does not fit the condition of lowest cost. io2 Block Express is for workloads that need sub-millisecond latency and high IOPS, so it is excessive for sequential processing.

prompt: The ALB RequestCount metric at an online ticket sales company runs to tens of thousands per minute during weekday daytime and drops to a few hundred in the early morning and on weekends. If a fixed threshold is set based on daytime, anomalies in the early morning are missed, and if it is set based on early morning, false positives are frequent during the day. This daily and weekly pattern has repeated in the same shape for several weeks. The operations team does not want to adjust thresholds by time of day by hand. The metric has already accumulated more than 5 weeks in CloudWatch, notifications can go to the existing SNS topic, and the team is interested in deviations in both directions from the normal range. Which method, among those that learn the day-of-week and time-of-day pattern and notify only when the metric leaves the normal range, has the LEAST operational overhead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fix a high threshold to match the daytime peak, and handle early-morning false positives by changing the alarm action to only log records instead of SNS.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Run a Lambda function every hour that calculates the average for the same day of week and time of day last month and publishes it as a custom metric, and set a fixed-threshold alarm on that metric.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create a composite alarm that combines the request count alarm and the CPU alarm with OR so that it notifies when either one fires, reducing missed detections.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enable an anomaly detection model on the RequestCount metric, and create an anomaly detection alarm that goes to ALARM when the metric leaves the expected range band.

explanation: The correct answer is an anomaly detection alarm. CloudWatch anomaly detection learns the time-of-day and day-of-week seasonality and trends from the metric's historical data to build a band of expected values, and the alarm fires when the metric goes above or below the band, so it meets the requirement without a fixed threshold. A fixed threshold based on daytime will never catch early-morning anomalies. Calculating and publishing averages with Lambda can work, but you must maintain the code, schedule, and seasonality adjustments yourself, so the operational burden is large. A composite alarm only combines existing alarm states and does not learn patterns, so it keeps the fixed-threshold problem.

prompt: An operations team at a company failed while updating a CloudFormation stack (with EC2, RDS, and S3 resources), and during the rollback, the attempt to restore the previous version of the RDS instance failed again, leaving the stack in the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state. Investigation showed that the cause was that, before the update, an operator had directly deleted that RDS instance from the console. This instance cannot be recovered, and the remaining EC2 and S3 resources are in production, so the stack cannot be deleted. The operations team has not manually touched any resources since the rollback failure, and the latest snapshot of the deleted instance is kept separately. What is the MOST appropriate action to return the stack to a state in which it can be updated again?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Run UpdateStack again with the same template to create the deleted RDS instance anew, thereby bypassing the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state. Review the impact in advance with a change set before running it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Call ContinueUpdateRollback and specify the logical ID of the RDS resource that failed to roll back in ResourcesToSkip, and then bring the template and the actual resources into agreement afterward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delete the entire stack, create a new stack with the same template, and manually migrate the running EC2 and S3 resources to the new stack.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Run drift detection on the stack so that the deleted RDS instance is automatically recovered based on the template and the rollback continues.

explanation: The correct answer is to specify the failed resource in ResourcesToSkip with ContinueUpdateRollback. When the cause of the rollback failure (the RDS instance deleted outside CloudFormation) cannot be fixed, you can skip that resource and return the stack to UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE, and because the skipped resource will be out of sync with the template, you must reconcile it before the next update. A stack in the UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED state cannot be updated, so running UpdateStack again with the same template is rejected. Deleting and recreating the stack requires moving running resources, which affects the service, and violates the constraint that the problem states the stack cannot be deleted. Drift detection only reports differences and does not recover resources or advance a rollback.

prompt: A StackSet at a company that has multiple business units deploys a logging bucket stack to 30 accounts in AWS Organizations. One business unit is being spun off, so the stacks in its 3 accounts must be removed from StackSet management, but the resources in those accounts, including the buckets that contain the logs accumulated so far, must continue to run as they are. After the transition, the business unit's own staff will operate those accounts directly, and the remaining 27 accounts will continue to be managed with the StackSet as they are now. The logging buckets contain logs under a retention policy, and if the buckets disappear because the stacks are deleted, it would be a compliance violation. What is the MOST appropriate method that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delete the stack instances without any options, and then manually create the same stack anew in those accounts from the same template.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deploy an update that removes the logging bucket resource from the StackSet template to all accounts to exclude it from management. Make sure it is reflected identically in all 30 accounts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Run an operation to delete the stack instances in those 3 accounts while selecting the Retain stacks option.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Delete the entire StackSet, then create a new StackSet for the remaining 27 accounts and redeploy.

explanation: When you delete stack instances and select the Retain stacks option, the stacks in those accounts and Regions are detached from the StackSet but the stacks and resources are left in place, so they can then be managed independently in the target accounts. Deleting without the option deletes resources such as the buckets along with the stacks and could lose the accumulated logs, and a newly created stack would not take over the existing resources. An update that removes the resource from the template applies to all stack instances, so the buckets in all 30 accounts would become targets for deletion. Deleting the entire StackSet and redeploying creates unnecessary change risk for the remaining accounts too.

prompt: An application server (10.0.5.20) in a newly created subnet times out when connecting to port 3306 on a database server in another subnet of the same VPC. The company wants to determine with evidence, not guesswork, whether the cause is a security group, a network ACL, or routing. Changing server settings requires a change approval process that takes several days, and work that touches traffic on the production database server must be avoided. The two subnets have network ACLs associated with them that were created by different teams, and flow logs are not yet turned on. Which TWO actions narrow down the cause the fastest without touching server settings or traffic? (Select TWO.)

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turn on VPC flow logs on the database server's ENI to check whether 3306 traffic from the app server's address is ACCEPT or REJECT, along with the records by direction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reboot the app server and the database server so that open connection states are reset, and then try the connection again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Analyze the path between the two ENIs with Reachability Analyzer to identify the security group, network ACL, or routing component that blocks the path.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turn on Route 53 Resolver query logs to first check whether the app server resolves the database hostname to the correct IP address.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Use Traffic Mirroring to replicate all packets from the database server to a security appliance and analyze the packet captures in detail with a separate analysis tool. Review the results together with the security team.

explanation: The correct answers are Reachability Analyzer and VPC flow logs. Reachability Analyzer is a configuration analysis tool that does not send packets; if the destination is reachable it shows the hop-by-hop path, and if not it identifies the blocking component such as a security group, network ACL, or route table. However, it analyzes only the network configuration, so it cannot show whether the server OS firewall or the application is listening on the port, and if the configuration all comes back as allowed, that layer must be checked separately. This problem is about determining which of the security group, network ACL, or routing is the cause, so configuration analysis is sufficient. Flow logs record allowed and denied traffic as ACCEPT and REJECT, so they provide evidence of where the actual request is being denied. Traffic Mirroring is for packet-level analysis, is excessive here, and requires configuration changes. Resolver query logs are a tool for name resolution problems and differ from diagnosing a timeout when connecting by IP. A reboot provides no evidence.

prompt: A global gaming company has identical ALB-based stacks in the Seoul and N. Virginia Regions. Regardless of a user's country, each user must be connected to the Region with the faster network response, and if the ALB in one Region is unhealthy, that Region must be excluded from DNS responses. The Seoul and N. Virginia stacks already have synchronized data so that either side can handle requests, and there are no country-specific data residency regulations. The domain is already in a Route 53 hosted zone. The ALB in each Region has a /ping path for health checks, and latency-based routing must be applied at the DNS response stage. What is the MOST appropriate Route 53 configuration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use geolocation records to map Asian users to Seoul and North American users to N. Virginia, with the default location set to Seoul.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Create a latency-based record for each Region and associate that ALB's health check with each record.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Create weighted records at 50 to 50 so that both Regions receive traffic at the same ratio, and associate health checks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create failover records with Seoul as primary and N. Virginia as secondary, so that traffic goes to N. Virginia only when Seoul is unhealthy.

explanation: The correct answer is latency-based records per Region with health checks associated. Latency routing responds with the Region that has the lowest latency to the user when resources are in multiple Regions, and a record with an associated health check is excluded from responses when it is unhealthy, so both requirements are met. Geolocation routing sends users to a predefined place based on user location and does not guarantee the Region with the faster response. Weighted routing only splits by ratio and does not consider per-user latency. Failover routing is an active-passive configuration that uses only the primary Region, so even users in N. Virginia would go to Seoul.

prompt: An order management company runs MySQL that it installed directly on EC2 with a 500 GiB data volume, and it consistently requires an average of 12,000 IOPS. Single-digit millisecond latency is sufficient, and sub-millisecond latency or more than 60,000 IOPS is not needed. The database runs on a single instance and does not use read replicas. The company currently uses a gp2 volume, but costs are rising because it has inflated the capacity to get the IOPS. Snapshots are taken once a day, and the instance type's EBS bandwidth fully supports the required IOPS and throughput. Which EBS volume configuration meets the performance requirements at the LOWEST cost?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 500 GiB io2 Block Express volume with 12,000 IOPS provisioned to secure consistent sub-millisecond latency

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 500 GiB gp2 volume, covering 12,000 IOPS with burst performance

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 500 GiB gp3 volume with 12,000 IOPS provisioned

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 500 GiB st1 Throughput Optimized HDD volume, using steady throughput as a substitute for the IOPS requirement

explanation: gp3 provides 3,000 IOPS as a baseline and lets you provision additional IOPS at a ratio of 500 IOPS per GiB up to 80,000 IOPS, so you can set 12,000 IOPS on a 500 GiB volume. Single-digit millisecond latency is sufficient, and its price per GiB is 20% lower than gp2, so it meets the requirements at the lowest cost. io2 Block Express is for workloads that need sub-millisecond latency or performance beyond 80,000 IOPS, so it incurs unnecessary cost in this problem. gp2 has IOPS proportional to capacity, a baseline of 1,500 IOPS at 500 GiB and bursting only to 3,000 IOPS, so it cannot sustain 12,000 IOPS. st1 is an HDD with a maximum of about 500 IOPS, so it does not suit an IOPS-driven database.

prompt: A software company creates a golden AMI with OS patches and the company's security agent applied every month and deploys it to 8 accounts in the Seoul and Tokyo Regions. Currently, an engineer connects to an EC2 instance and creates and copies the AMI manually, and last month an image with missing patches was deployed. Only images that pass testing must be deployed, and the company wants to minimize the servers and scripts it must manage itself. The infrastructure team has 2 members. The test stage is already defined as running a CIS benchmark check script, and all 8 target accounts belong to the same organization. What is the MOST appropriate method that meets these requirements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Place a cron script on a build EC2 instance to create the AMI and use the AWS CLI to copy and share it to each Region and account.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Back up a reference instance every month with AWS Backup and copy the recovery points to other Regions and accounts to use as AMIs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Define an EC2 Image Builder pipeline with a monthly schedule, build and test components, and a distribution configuration that specifies the target Regions and accounts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Have an engineer manually enter the latest AMI ID into the ImageId parameter of the CloudFormation template every month to update the stack.
